items.why: Tests the meaningful contrast between Jeroboam’s unchanged conduct and his renewed priest appointments.
The unnamed “he” and a message that “will happen” make the question awkward and unclear.
Distinguishes the collective defeat of four descendants from Jonathan’s individual victory.
Requires tracking the officer through the quoted exchange to identify who is trampled.
Clearly distinguishes the rider from those saddling the donkey, but tests a minor travel action.
Tests the important difference in participants between the two covenants.
Separates Jotham’s succession from the preceding note about Isaiah’s historical record.
Distinguishes Uzziah’s stated reason for leaving from the priests’ action toward him.
Presents the king’s suspected trap as the Arameans’ established plan.
Tests the men’s chosen course against an explicitly rejected alternative.
“Who kills first” tests incidental narrative order rather than a substantial distinction.
The question is vague, and “the news” does not explain what was reported.
Clearly tests whom the king targets with the command “Seize him!”
The referent is clear, but the competitor is already named among those following him.
Requires tracking the two mothers’ children through nested speech and contrasting days.
Distinguishes Uzziah’s religious instructor from his father and moral example.
Separates Elisha’s response to the officer’s doubt from his earlier price prediction.
Tests the divine prohibition behind the refusal rather than a supposed inadequate reward.
Requires placing Paul’s continued speech after the meal and immediately before departure.
Asks only for the first action in a plainly ordered list of military preparations.
Distinguishes the person distributing the weapons from their former owner.
The accusers–council distinction is clear, but “the addressee” is unnecessarily stilted.
“Take” is vague, and the competitor gives a cause rather than the requested purpose.
Tests the distinction between commanding the troops and mustering their numbers.
Requires distinguishing the two prophets to identify the lion’s victim.
Duplicates the officer’s trampling already tested more strongly by Q89C41.
Useful duty-group distinction, but the key should include both on-duty and off-duty companies.
Requires distinguishing the letter’s named sender from its named recipient.
Clearly distinguishes the enemy Abishai kills from the person he rescues.
Tests the shift from concealing loot to reporting good news after recognizing wrongdoing.
Distinguishes the young informant from Paul, who arranges his access to the commander.
Tests the report immediately preceding the plundering rather than the earlier reconnaissance.
The phrasing is stilted and makes a minor, easily resolved pronoun the main target.
Requires identifying whose child was eaten through the woman’s first-person account.
Distinguishes the person requesting prayer from the person who actually intercedes.
Separates the enemies God helps defeat from the Ammonites who bring tribute.
The city and its tomb are nested destinations, making “first” a weak contrast.
“Ahaziah’s son’s nurse” is convoluted and effectively supplies the hidden person’s identity.
Distinguishes the stated cause of calm from the people’s accompanying rejoicing.
Tests the difference between officers receiving orders and soldiers being prepared.
Distinguishes the imagined attackers from the king believed to have hired them.
Requires distinguishing the ruler ordering the killing from the messenger carrying it out.
Tracks the intended guest through the old prophet’s quoted claim.
The reason is explicit, while the lamps offer a particularly implausible competing explanation.
Tests which escort group returns and which continues accompanying Paul.
Requires tracking attacker and victims through several pronouns to identify who flees.
Illnesses also cease, so “what leaves” mainly tests matching the passage’s exact verb.
Distinguishes the commander expected to bring Paul from the council requesting him.
“Assembling materials” needlessly obscures the straightforward action of gathering scrolls.
Separates the explicit sword order concerning followers from the woman’s later execution.
Distinguishes what prompts Athaliah’s arrival from what she sees after arriving.
Distinguishes the authorization awaited by the plotters from the proposed council appearance.
The speaker–recipient distinction is useful, but “whose body is warned” is grammatically awkward.
Distinguishes the future son named in the prophecy from the king currently at the altar.
